meta: Agnolo Bronzino's Saint John the Baptist, about 1542 to 1545, a twisting figure from a triptych in Eleonora di Toledo's private chapel.
about: Saint John the Baptist twists inside a tall, narrow panel, his torso turned so that his limbs zigzag in strong diagonals from top to bottom. He wears an animal skin over a pink-red drapery and holds a slender wooden cross. The panel is tall for a reason. The Getty explains that it was part of a triptych altarpiece in the private chapel of Eleonora di Toledo in the Palazzo Vecchio. Bronzino's artificial, serpentine pose marks his move in the 1540s away from naturalism toward more stylized, elongated forms. A small bowl rests on the rocks at lower right.

meta: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo's Alexander the Great and Campaspe in the Studio of Apelles, about 1740, a story of a painter who fell for his sitter.
about: A young painter gazes at the woman whose portrait he is working on. He is Apelles, whom ancient writers ranked as the greatest artist of his time, and she is Campaspe, Alexander the Great's favorite. The Getty gives the story as Pliny tells it. Alexander commissioned the portrait. Apelles fell in love with his sitter as he captured her beauty on canvas. Alexander so esteemed his painter that he gave Campaspe to him as a reward. Tiepolo sets the scene in a colonnaded classical studio. The painter works at an easel.

meta: Johann Zoffany's conversation piece of Lord Willoughby de Broke and his family at tea, painted about 1766.
about: A family is about to take tea. John Peyto-Verney, the fourteenth Lord Willoughby de Broke, sits with his wife Lady Louisa North and their three young children around a table of porcelain and a silver samovar. She holds their daughter, who stands on the table trying a first step. One son enters on the right pulling a red toy horse. Another reaches for a piece of buttered bread while his father gestures a warning. The Getty says Zoffany was especially good at conversation pieces, which are informal group portraits of lively figures in carefully detailed rooms.

meta: Bachiacca's Portrait of a Woman with a Book of Music, about 1540 to 1545, a Florentine sitter in fashionable dress holding printed music.
about: A young woman in a pink dress with full, fur-trimmed sleeves sits beside a green table and holds open a book of music. Her dress was the height of Florentine fashion around 1540, and the Getty reads her costume and music book as signs of a cultured, patrician background. Her name is unknown. The painting once belonged to the Frescobaldi, a powerful Florentine banking family, and the museum suggests she may have been one of them. A painted border of songbirds runs across the tablecloth.

meta: William Blake's 1795 Satan Exulting over Eve, a color print finished with watercolor washes.
about: Satan hovers over Eve in a blaze of red while the serpent of the Garden of Eden coils around her. The Getty looks closely at how it was made. The uneven, fibrous color under Eve shows that the area was printed, and the even sweep of red washes shows that the flames behind Satan are mostly watercolor. Blake often chose watercolor because he liked how transparent it is. The museum quotes him insisting that his visions were organized and minutely articulated.

meta: Pellegrino Tibaldi's pen drawing of the Incredulity of Thomas, with a study for Thomas on the back, made about 1565 to 1585.
about: Christ strides forward in a radiant glow, his cape billowing, while a kneeling apostle reaches toward him. The scene comes from the Gospel story of Thomas, who missed Jesus's first appearance after the Resurrection and refused to believe until he saw the wounds. When Christ returned, he told Thomas to touch the nail holes in his hands and the gash in his side. Tibaldi characteristically used a nervously energetic line, the Getty says. Pen and brown ink, brown wash and white heightening build the figures. A study for Thomas is on the back of the sheet.

meta: Fernand Khnopff's 1885 portrait of Jeanne Kéfer, the daughter of a composer friend, standing small before a tall door.
about: A small girl in a bonnet and brown coat stands before a pale green door, her thumb catching the edge of her bow as she reaches into her coat. Jeanne Kéfer was the daughter of a composer friend of Khnopff. The Getty reads the small gesture as a sign of the child's vulnerability and uncertainty in facing the outside world. To suggest a child's view of a world built for grown-ups, he set her tiny body against an adult-sized door and tilted the floor ever so slightly. The brushwork in the door's window behind her is free and abstract.

meta: Willem van Aelst's 1674 still life of dead birds, a kingfisher among them, laid beside a green velvet game bag.
about: Dead birds lie on dark satin beside a green velvet game bag and a wicker basket. Van Aelst painted them so carefully that the Getty can name each one. The blue-green bird is a kingfisher, the small red one a Eurasian bullfinch, and the yellow-brown one a male bearded tit. Few Dutch artists painted dead game and fowl, perhaps because hunting was not widely practiced in the northern Netherlands. A small number of such pictures began to appear in Holland around 1640, but the market stayed small. Van Aelst gave the birds the same care he gave crystal goblets and silver platters in his luxury still lifes.

meta: Gerard David's Holy Family, about 1520, set in a Netherlandish interior with apples, a bowl of milk porridge and a castle view.
about: The Virgin holds the Christ Child tightly while Joseph looks on from behind. Christ clasps an unblemished apple, which the Getty reads as a sign that he is the new Adam. Joseph holds a lidded wooden bowl that keeps the child's porridge-like milk warm. Two decaying apples sit on the lid. The museum sees them as a hint of the Passion to come. David set the family in a contemporary Netherlandish interior with a view of hilly country and a castle. The museum says this addressed the taste for everyday subjects among patrons in the Antwerp art market.

meta: Jean-Étienne Liotard's pastel portrait of the Baron de Lubières, drawn on both sides of the sheet, about 1760.
about: A fashionably dressed man sits in profile with a fur muff in his hand. Liotard drew him on both sides of a thin cream sheet. On the back he applied red and black pastels to give the finely detailed front richer and subtler tone and relief. The Getty says the technique appears in several of his portraits of the period and comes from the habit of toning ivory miniatures on the verso. The sitter, Charles-Benjamin de Langes de Montmirail, was a wealthy, learned amateur in Voltaire's circle in Geneva who contributed several articles to Diderot's Encyclopédie. Against a plain background, nothing distracts from the likeness.

meta: Paolo Veronese's Portrait of a Man, about 1576 to 1578, a full-length sitter whose name is not known.
about: A bearded man in black, with a white ruff and cuffs, leans on a classical column and holds a feathered hat. His name is lost. At one point scholars thought the painting might be a self-portrait, but the sitter's face differs somewhat from Veronese's early self-portrait in the Hermitage, so the idea is unconfirmed. The Getty adds that the architecture and a half-visible marble figure in a niche may point to his profession, perhaps sculptor or architect. Veronese was once regarded as Venice's greatest portraitist, and Vasari admired his portraits.

meta: Volterrano's red chalk Wine Jest, about 1640, a drawing of the priest Arlotto Mainardi leaving a barrel spigot open.
about: A priest raises his fist and the men at the table react in different ways. He is Arlotto Mainardi, a notorious prankster, and the drawing shows his trick on his companions. Sent to the cellar for wine, he expected them to eat his share of the food while he was away, so he left the barrel spigot open. Volterrano drew it in red chalk and squared it for transfer to canvas. It served as a modello for one of his most famous paintings, now in the Palazzo Pitti in Florence. His contemporaries admired the composition and made many copies.

meta: Jean-Marc Nattier's 1742 portrait of Madame Bonnier de la Mosson dressed as Diana, goddess of the hunt.
about: Madame Bonnier de la Mosson sits as Diana, goddess of the moon, the forest and the hunt, holding a bow and arrow and wrapped in a leopard skin. Behind her are a dramatic sky and a barren landscape. She ran a literary salon in Paris that drew the most noted people of her day. In eighteenth-century France it was fashionable for aristocratic women to have their portraits made in mythological or historical roles. The Getty says Nattier, one of the leading portraitists of his day, specialized in these flattering allegories. He painted most of the circle around Louis XV and Madame de Pompadour.

meta: Adriaen van de Venne's 1615 Merry Company in an Arbor, a small landscape of musicians and youths spying on women.
about: Maidens make music under a flowery arbor at the left of this small landscape. On the right two women sit on a net used to catch finches, and youths spy on them from trees and bushes. One bold voyeur clings to the top of the arbor. Another gets tangled in a net and is caught by a soberly dressed woman, while two jesters fall out of the trees. The Getty calls the picture light-hearted. It was one of a series of four landscapes of the seasons, and this one is thought to stand for spring. Its companion, a ball game before a country palace, also carries imagery of love.

meta: Anthony van Dyck's oil sketch of Saint Sebastian tended by an angel, about 1630 to 1632, probably made for a painting never finished.
about: Saint Sebastian, tied to a tree and shot with arrows, barely notices the angel who is helping to remove them. Van Dyck painted the saint many times but never stressed the arrows in the flesh. The Getty says he was after emotional possibilities. He worked in thin paint and grisaille, sketching in the composition quickly and testing how light and shadow fall on the torso and the angel's body. This is an oil sketch for a painting that was probably never finished or is now lost. Rubens first developed the Flemish oil sketch as an alternative to drawing, and Van Dyck, his most gifted pupil, soon took it up.

meta: Anthony van Dyck's Portrait of Agostino Pallavicini, painted in 1621 for the future doge of Genoa.
about: Agostino Pallavicini sits in a carved chair wrapped in the flowing red robes he wore as ambassador to the pope. The fabric spreads so widely that it nearly takes over the painting. Van Dyck painted him in 1621, soon after leaving Antwerp for Italy, where he stayed for five years. It was one of his first Italian paintings. The Getty says it commemorates Pallavicini's service as ambassador to the newly elected Pope Gregory XV. The coat of arms on the drapery at the left confirms who he is. He later became doge of Genoa.

meta: Bartolomeo Cavarozzi's Supper at Emmaus, about 1615 to 1625, a close copy of Caravaggio's version now in the National Gallery, London.
about: Christ reveals himself to Cleophas and Saint Peter at a table while the innkeeper looks on. The Getty thinks Cavarozzi painted this picture after Caravaggio's treatment of the subject, now in the National Gallery in London. In the 1600s the original was in Rome, where many artists saw and copied it. Cavarozzi follows it closely, with differences. The three figures around Christ are reversed and seen from a slightly lower viewpoint, which makes them more monumental. The composition is more symmetrical and has less depth, and the still life of grapes, bread and fish is enlarged.

meta: Agostino Carracci's Cupid Overpowering Pan, about 1590, a study for a fireplace fresco in Bologna's Palazzo Magnani.
about: Cupid wrestles the goat-legged god Pan in this black chalk study on blue-grey paper. Agostino Carracci made it for a fresco over a fireplace in Bologna's Palazzo Magnani, where he, his brother Annibale and their cousin Ludovico decorated rooms in the early 1590s. Many of their works are still there. The story shows love overcoming lust, and it illustrates Virgil's line Omnia vincit Amor, love conquers all. On the back is a head of a monk, studied for the priest in his painting of the Last Communion of Saint Jerome. The soft modeling and the extreme foreshortening of Cupid's head show his interest in Venetian art.

meta: Christoph Murer's 1592 design for a stained glass window with the Ecce Homo, made for the Swiss abbey of Rathausen.
about: Pilate shows the thorn-crowned Christ to a jeering crowd and gazes out at the viewer as if to implicate him. The drawing is a design for a stained glass window. Below are the arms of two Lucerne families who commissioned it: the Kündigs and the Pfyffers. The Virgin and Child, King Caspar and angels with instruments of the Passion surround the scene. It belongs to a large series of designs for the cloister of the Cistercian abbey of Rathausen in the canton of Lucerne. The windows were made between 1592 and 1623, and Franz Fallenter made them until 1611.

meta: Agnolo Bronzino's black chalk Study of Jealousy, about 1545, a drawing of hands and an arm made for his Allegory of Venus and Cupid.
about: A bare-chested figure tilts his head and grips his skull with both hands. The hands and the muscular arm are the real subject. Face and torso are barely sketched. Bronzino made the drawing as a study for the figure of Jealousy in his painting Allegory of Venus and Cupid. He drew from a studio model and placed the model's hands and arms with care. An X-ray of the painting shows that he first painted the hands higher and more horizontal across the head, so he probably settled the pose in this drawing and then went back to rework the painting.

meta: Jan Brueghel the Elder's 1613 painting of animals streaming toward Noah's ark, made while he was court painter in the Southern Netherlands.
about: Animals of every kind crowd the earth and sky as Noah herds them toward a distant ark. Large elephants lumber past while turtles and hamsters sit in the foreground. Bats and birds cross the sky. Brueghel painted it while he was court painter to Archduke Albert and the Infanta Isabella, who ruled the Southern Netherlands. The Getty says the story suited his descriptive skill. It links the range of species to the curiosity about the natural world that the exploration of the Americas in the 1500s had spurred.

meta: Urs Graf's 1525 pen drawing of a dancing peasant couple, signed with his initials and the Swiss dagger.
about: Two peasants dance so closely that their bodies make a figure eight, and the man hides his partner's head while pinching her buttock. Urs Graf drew them on a bare strip of ground and signed the sheet with his initials crossed by the Swiss dagger. The Getty says peasants were then commonly seen as symbols of the cycles of nature, earthy and fertile, and often bawdy. The drawing is pricked with holes along the figures' outlines. Scholars once took that as a sign of a design for a print. They now believe another draftsman pricked it much later in order to copy it.

meta: Francisco Ribalta's pen drawing of the Coronation of the Virgin, made about 1600 to 1628, probably a study for an altar painting.
about: Angels tumble around the Virgin Mary as she accepts the crown as Queen of Heaven. Christ and an angel lower it toward her head, and a dove of the Holy Spirit hovers above. The Getty notes that the Coronation of the Virgin was a popular subject in Catholic circles, especially in Spain. Ribalta drew it in pen and brown ink and added wash to strengthen the vigorous pen work and pull the composition together. The sheet has an arched top. That suggests he made it in preparation for an altar painting.

meta: Orazio Gentileschi's Danaë and the Shower of Gold, painted 1621 to 1623 for Giovanni Antonio Sauli's palace in Genoa.
about: Danaë reclines on a gilded bed as Cupid draws back a dark green curtain to let Jupiter enter as a shower of gold. Gentileschi made it in 1622 as one of a group of works for Giovanni Antonio Sauli's palace in Genoa. The group includes the Getty's Lot and His Daughters and a Penitent Magdalene now in a private collection. The subject comes from Ovid's Metamorphoses. King Acrisius locked up his daughter to avoid a prophecy that her son would kill him. The Getty observes that the viewer is invited to witness the moment of seduction.

meta: The Man with the Golden Helmet, about 1650, a Berlin portrait long given to Rembrandt and now placed in his circle.
about: A bust-length older man looks downward from a nearly black background. He wears a gilded helmet with a dark feathered plume and a polished breastplate over dark clothes. For a long time the picture was given to Rembrandt. Today it is considered the work of someone in his circle. The Gemäldegalerie in Berlin owns it.

meta: Lorenzo Lotto's Portrait of a Young Man, about 1526, signed L. Lotus pict. and later bought for the Prussian king Frederick William III.
about: A young man with a dark beard and a black beret looks out in front of a red curtain, which parts at the right to show a harbor scene, perhaps the Venetian lagoon. Lotto signed it L. Lotus pict. and probably painted it about 1526, soon after returning to Venice from Bergamo. A 1638 inventory lists it in the collection of Marquess Vincenzo Giustiniani. In 1815 it was sold through a Paris dealer, Féréol Bonnemaison, to Frederick William III of Prussia. Old inventories record a marble balustrade in the foreground that was later removed. Two fingertips remain, once painted black and uncovered again in a restoration.

meta: Hans Holbein the Younger's 1533 portrait of Hermann Hillebrandt de Wedigh, a Cologne man thought to be a merchant in London.
about: A bearded man in a black cap and dark cloak stands against a bright blue background and holds a rolled paper in one hand. Hans Holbein the Younger painted him in 1533 in oil and tempera on oak. The sitter, Hermann Hillebrandt de Wedigh, belonged to the Wedigh family of Cologne. He is thought to have been a merchant of the Steelyard in London. The portrait is now in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin.

meta: Johannes Vermeer's The Wine Glass, about 1660, a woman and a man drinking wine in a bright Delft interior.
about: A woman in red satin raises a wine glass while a man in a wide-brimmed black hat looks toward her across a table spread with a patterned carpet. Vermeer painted it about 1660. The picture follows the conventions of Delft School genre painting as Pieter de Hooch developed them in the late 1650s. Its figures sit in a brightly lit, spacious room with sharply defined architecture, and they are placed in the middle ground instead of the usual foreground. Wikipedia lists two other titles, The Glass of Wine and Lady and Gentleman Drinking Wine.

meta: Peter Paul Rubens's Ecce Homo of about 1612, a Christ crowned with thorns, once owned by Prince Bezborodko in Saint Petersburg.
about: Christ wears a crown of thorns, his bare torso marked with wounds and his hands bound with a reed. Rubens painted the panel about 1612 for Cardinal Massimego, and Christ's pose was influenced by an ancient statue of a centaur in the Borghese Gallery in Rome. By the end of the eighteenth century it was in Prince Bezborodko's collection in Saint Petersburg. It passed to his relatives by marriage, the Counts Kushelev, and in 1862 Count Nikolai Kushelev-Bezborodko left the collection to the Academy of Arts. The Hermitage also holds an oil study for the figure of Pilate.

meta: Peter Paul Rubens and his studio's Venus and Adonis, about 1614, a Hermitage version of a 1609 picture now in Düsseldorf.
about: Venus embraces a young Adonis, who holds a spear and wears a flowing red cloak, while a cupid and hunting dogs gather near. This is a version of an earlier work by Rubens from 1609, now in the Museum Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf. The rocky background there is replaced with Venus's attribute, a golden chariot. Rubens painted the main figures himself. His students did the rest. The landscape is now attributed to Lucas van Uden or Jan Wildens, and Wildens painted the dogs. The picture was in private collections in Brussels, including Carl de Cobenzel's, until a collector sold it to the Hermitage in 1768.

meta: Lorenzo di Credi's circular panel of Mary adoring the Christ Child with the infant John the Baptist, dated 1480.
about: Mary kneels in prayer in a blue mantle with a green lining while the infant Christ lies on a cushion and the infant John the Baptist kneels in prayer beside him. The Kunsthalle in Karlsruhe says Lorenzo di Credi used a round format, called a tondo. In the Renaissance this shape was often chosen for pictures of Mary, since the circle could be read as a symbol of perfection and harmony.

meta: Hans Baldung's 1528 Unequal Pair of Lovers, an old man and a young woman holding gold coins, a theme he first used in 1507.
about: A white-haired old man in a brown coat and gold chain rests his hand on the shoulder of a younger woman. She holds gold coins in her lap. The Unequal Pair is a theme Baldung returned to several times. He used it as early as 1507 in an engraving, and its roots lie in ancient poetry. Here he used it for a panel painting, as the Kunsthalle Karlsruhe points out. The woman wears a white dress with orange sleeves and a dark netted hairnet.

meta: Paolo Veronese's Lucretia, about 1580 to 1583, a Venetian painting of the Roman woman at the moment she takes her own life.
about: Lucretia looks downward in a green velvet gown and gold-trimmed overdress, adorned with pearls and gold bracelets, as she holds a dagger hidden in her fabric. The scene shows her about to pierce her chest after the king's son Sextus Tarquinius raped her. Many artists painted the subject, among them Titian, Rembrandt and Raphael. Wikipedia singles out Veronese's attention to detail, from the drapery that cloaks her to her jewels. The picture is in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.

meta: A workshop painting after Anthony van Dyck, 1630 to 1632, of Thetis receiving the weapons of Achilles from Hephaestus.
about: Thetis, in a red drape and silver breastplate, receives armor for her son Achilles from the smith god Hephaestus while putti handle helmets and weapons. The scene illustrates the shield of Achilles in Book 18 of the Iliad, where Thetis asks Hephaestus for replacement arms for her son. The painting comes from the workshop of Anthony van Dyck. Archduke Leopold Wilhelm of Austria acquired it. It is now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.
